---
title: Quarto-Hub auth model
---

# The one idea to keep in your head

The hub server **verifies** identity; it does not **broker** it.

Almost every "how does OAuth work" mental model assumes a confidential
server that holds a `client_secret`, redirects you to Google, and exchanges
an authorization code for tokens behind the scenes. **The Quarto-Hub server
does none of that.** The entire OAuth dance happens between your *browser*
and *Google*. The hub only ever receives a Google-signed ID token (a JWT),
checks that Google really signed it, and checks that you're allowed in. It
never talks to Google's token endpoint, and it holds no OAuth client secret.

Everything below is an elaboration of that one sentence.

# The players

- **The browser + Google Identity Services (GIS).** The SPA embeds Google's
  `gsi/client` script (via `@react-oauth/google`). This is what actually runs
  the OAuth flow, mints the ID token, and hands it back.
- **The hub binary** (`crates/quarto-hub`, shipped as `hub` / `quarto hub`).
  A pure OIDC *verifier*. All auth code lives in one module,
  `crates/quarto-hub/src/auth.rs`, with the HTTP wiring in `server.rs` and
  the per-request check in `context.rs`.
- **nginx**, on the deployment box, terminating TLS and reverse-proxying to
  the hub on `127.0.0.1:3000`. The hub is never directly reachable from the
  internet.
- **Google's JWKS endpoint.** The hub downloads Google's *public* signing
  keys once at startup and refreshes them in the background. Verification is
  entirely local after that — there is no per-request round-trip to Google.

Auth is **optional and off by default**. It turns on only when the hub is
started with `--oidc-client-id` (env `OIDC_CLIENT_ID`). With no client ID,
the SPA mounts a no-op auth provider and everyone is anonymous.

# Signing in: unauthenticated → authenticated

1. The browser loads the SPA. On mount it calls `GET /auth/me`. With no
   session cookie yet, the hub answers **401**, and the SPA shows the login
   screen.
2. You click "Sign in with Google". The GIS button is configured in
   *redirect* mode with `login_uri = <origin>/auth/callback`. The browser
   navigates to Google; GIS also drops a short-lived `g_csrf_token` cookie on
   the hub's origin.
3. You authenticate/consent at Google. **Google then POSTs a form directly to
   `/auth/callback`** carrying two fields: `credential` (the ID-token JWT) and
   `g_csrf_token`.
4. The hub's `/auth/callback` handler:
   - **CSRF check (double-submit):** the `g_csrf_token` form field must equal
     the `g_csrf_token` cookie. Mismatch → redirect to `/?auth_error`.
   - **Verifies the JWT** (see next section).
   - On success, sets the session cookie and **redirects to a clean `/`**.
5. The SPA reloads, `GET /auth/me` now returns **200** with
   `{ email, name, picture, exp }`, and the app renders.
6. Before opening a project, the SPA calls `GET /auth/actor?project=<id>` to
   get its per-project automerge actor ID (see below), then opens the sync
   WebSocket.

`/auth/callback` is only registered for the Google form-POST flow. A generic
OIDC front-end would instead POST its own freshly-minted token to
`/auth/refresh`.

# The session *is* the JWT

There is **no server-side session store.** The Google-signed JWT is the
session token, stored verbatim in a cookie:

- Name: `quarto_hub_token`
- `HttpOnly` (JavaScript can never read it), `SameSite=Lax`, `Path=/`
- `Secure` (unless explicitly running with `--allow-insecure-auth`)
- `Max-Age=3600` — **one hour**

On every request the hub re-verifies this JWT from scratch. There is nothing
to "look up" — validity is a pure function of the token plus Google's public
keys plus the allowlist.

## What "verify" actually checks

The verification pipeline (`context.rs` → `auth.rs`) enforces, in order:

1. **Signature** against Google's cached JWKS keys.
2. **Standard claims** — `exp` (expiry), `nbf`, issuer
   (`https://accounts.google.com`), and **audience**. The accepted audience
   set is the configured `--oidc-client-id` *plus* any `--additional-audiences`
   (this is how the `q2 mcp` desktop client is allowed to share the hub).
3. **`azp` + `iat`** — the OIDC authorized-party rule, plus rejection of
   tokens with a future `iat`.
4. **Allowlists** — `email_verified` must be true, and the email must match
   the configured `--allowed-emails` or `--allowed-domains` (currently:
   `posit.co` and a short list of individual addresses).

Who signs, who verifies: **Google signs, the hub verifies.** The hub never
issues a signature of its own — the cookie is just Google's JWT, unmodified.

## Two ways to present a credential

- **Cookie** — browsers, automatically, on every request.
- **`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`** — non-browser clients (the
  `quarto-hub-mcp` server). Sending *both* a cookie and a Bearer header on the
  same request is rejected with a 400.

Cookie-based state-changing requests additionally require an
`X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest` header (a second CSRF defense);
`/auth/callback` can't use that trick because it's a cross-origin POST from
Google, which is why it relies on the double-submit cookie instead.

# Staying signed in (silent refresh)

The cookie lives one hour, but the session outlives it via silent renewal.
Roughly 15 minutes before expiry the SPA uses GIS One-Tap to mint a fresh ID
token in the background and POSTs it to `/auth/refresh`, which re-verifies it
and re-sets the cookie. No user interaction, no redirect.

# Authorizing sync over the WebSocket

The SPA syncs automerge documents over a WebSocket at `/ws` (nginx proxies it
with a 24-hour idle timeout). Two things are worth understanding here, and the
second is the important one for a security review.

**Authentication happens once, at upgrade time.** When the WebSocket
connection is established, the hub validates the credential (the cookie rides
along automatically) using the *same* verification pipeline as HTTP requests.
Cookie-based upgrades also get an `Origin`-vs-`Host` check to block
cross-origin WebSocket hijacking. **Trade-off:** the token is checked only at
connection time. A user whose token expires (or is revoked) on an
*already-open* connection is not forcibly disconnected — the client
re-authenticates when it notices expiry and reconnects.

**Authorization is capability-based, not an access-control list.** This is the
part that most surprises people. The hub's samod access policy
(`access_policy.rs`) is an **audit policy**: its "is this peer allowed to
touch this document?" check **always returns true.** It only *logs* the first
time each `(user, document)` pair is seen, tagged with the user's email.

In other words: **any authenticated user who knows a document's automerge ID
can sync it.** There is no per-project membership check on the server. Access
to a project is controlled by *knowledge of its (unguessable) index document
ID* — which is exactly what a Quarto-Hub share URL contains. Sharing is
handing someone the ID; the server does not maintain a separate "who's on this
project" list. (This is the same capability model the MCP tooling describes:
"the link users share to grant access.")

So the two gates compose like this:

- **Authentication** (are you a known, allowlisted human?) — enforced by
  Google's signature + the email/domain allowlist.
- **Authorization** (may you touch *this* project?) — enforced by whether you
  possess its document ID. The server audit-logs, but does not adjudicate.

# Per-project actor IDs (an aside, not a gate)

Before opening documents, the SPA fetches `GET /auth/actor?project=<id>`. The
hub returns
`HMAC-SHA256(server_secret, sub || "\0" || project_id)` — a stable automerge
actor ID that is:

- **Per-user** (derived from the Google `sub`),
- **Per-project** (can't be correlated across projects),
- **Unforgeable** without the server secret.

This is an *attribution/isolation* mechanism — it gives each collaborator a
consistent identity inside a project's edit history — **not** an authorization
check. See `data-model.qmd` for how the resulting identities show up in the
project index document.

# Secrets inventory (for reviewers)

Worth being explicit about what is and isn't secret:

| Thing | Secret? | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Google **client ID** | No (public identifier) | Baked into the SPA at build time (`VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`); passed to the hub as `--oidc-client-id`. Marked `sensitive` in Terraform out of caution, but it's a public value. |
| Google **client secret** | — | **Does not exist in this system.** The hub is not a confidential client and never performs a code exchange. |
| Session signing key | — | **Does not exist.** Google signs the JWT; the hub only verifies. |
| `QUARTO_HUB_SERVER_SECRET` | **Yes** | HMAC key for per-project actor IDs. Read from env → `hub.json` → auto-generated 32 random bytes. Unrelated to OAuth. |
| The session token | Yes (it's a bearer credential) | `HttpOnly` cookie, never exposed to JS. |
| A project's automerge index ID | **Yes, effectively** | It *is* the access capability. Anyone who has it can read/sync the project. Share URLs carry it. |

# Deployment trust boundaries

On the production box (a single AWS EC2 instance):

- **nginx terminates TLS** (Let's Encrypt cert for `quarto-hub.com`) and
  reverse-proxies `/auth`, `/api`, `/health`, and `/ws` to the hub on
  loopback. Static SPA assets are served directly by nginx from local disk.
- The hub runs with **`--behind-tls-proxy`** so it trusts
  `X-Forwarded-Proto` and sets `Secure` cookies correctly. With auth enabled,
  the hub *refuses to start* over plain HTTP unless you explicitly pass
  `--allow-insecure-auth`.
- The **allowlist** (`--allowed-domains` / `--allowed-emails` /
  `--additional-audiences`) is delivered as config, not baked into the binary,
  so who-may-sign-in can change without a redeploy of the server.
- The Google client ID reaches the box via a mode-600 env file
  (`/etc/quarto-hub/env`); the SPA carries the same ID baked in at build time.
  (Historical wrinkle: the server-side flag was renamed
  `--google-client-id` → `--oidc-client-id`, so the same value travels under
  the name `OIDC_CLIENT_ID` server-side and `VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` in the SPA
  build.)

# Known trade-offs, stated plainly

- **No per-document ACL.** Authorization = possession of the document ID.
  Revoking one person's access to one project is not currently a server
  operation.
- **WebSocket auth is upgrade-time only.** Expiry/revocation doesn't tear down
  live connections; it's caught on reconnect.
- **One-hour token, silent refresh.** Sign-out clears the cookie, but a leaked
  token is valid until it expires (up to an hour), and there is no server-side
  revocation list.
